transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (Mariner CTO), Mei Chen (Head of Platform), Tom Briggs (SRE)
---
00:00 Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining — looks like we have about 40 minutes, quick agenda: high-level Optimize walkthrough, batching recommendations, prefix/KV cache cost model, then open Q&A. Priya will lead the technical bits.
00:18 Priya (Redwood SE): yep hi all, uh thanks for the intro alex. quick context check — you told us earlier mariner is doing enrichment on transaction streams, mostly sub-second responses for risk scoring, is that right?
00:28 Carlos (Mariner CTO): yeah that's correct. we're enriching with several internal models plus third party lookups. latency is important, p95 ideally under 200ms for UI flows, for async background jobs we can tolerate more.
:45 Alex: and do you have a target request volume? we saw notes — around 4k to 10k rps peaks?
00:52 Mei: yeah peak bursts 6k rps, average more like 1k. most calls are short context — 32 to 128 tokens typical.
01:05 Priya: perfect. so the two levers we'll focus on are batching and KV/prefix caching. at a high level batching reduces amortized per-token cost by combining in-flight requests; caching avoids recomputation for repeated prefixes — common for similar transaction metadata. we'll show cost model numbers and tradeoffs.
01:30 Tom (SRE): one thing up front — security question: how does the KV cache live? is it within the redwood cluster or can we run in our VPC? we need KMS and audit logs.
01:42 Alex: good question. for private deployments we can host the cache in your VPC and integrate with customer KMS/HSM. for hosted we offer encrypted KV cache with SSE and audit logs; we'll share SOC2 docs.
01:55 Carlos: okay thanks.
---
03:00 Priya: demo slide 1 — batching basics. so there are two modes: continuous batching (low-latency, small batches) and windowed batching (higher throughput, higher latency). given your p95 target, we recommend continuous batching with dynamic batch sizing tuned to your traffic profile.
03:25 Priya: example: at 1k RPS, continuous batching with max batch size 32 and latency SLO 200ms gives about 1.8x token cost reduction vs no batching. if you use windowed batching to maximize throughput you could hit 3-4x but with p95 up by 80-120ms.
03:50 Mei: those numbers assume what model? 7B? 13B?
03:55 Priya: good catch — example used an open 13B variant with quantization q4; for a 7B the proportional improvement is similar but absolute token time is lower. we'll include model-specific slides.
04:10 Alex: note also model kernel selection affects CPU vs GPU utility — our runtime picks kernels by architecture and sequence length so these numbers vary a bit.
---
06:00 Priya: next is prefix and KV cache. two patterns: prefix cache stores model KV states for a common prefix (like repeated system prompt + user metadata), KV cache stores intermediate KV states for exact past sequences. prefix is higher hit rate for standard prompts.
06:25 Priya: cost model: assume 10% cache hit rate on prefixes with K=128 tokens saved per hit; with your traffic that roughly maps to a 12-18% token cost reduction at baseline, combined with batching you can see 30-45% lower unit cost.
06:50 Tom: do cached entries expire? what about invalidation when prompt templates change?
07:00 Priya: yes TTL-based invalidation, and we provide semantic keys — you can version prefixes. for template changes you can bump the prefix version so old entries are ignored. we also support manual invalidation via API.
07:20 Carlos: what about memory size? how big is the cache per model?
07:25 Priya: depends on kv per token and model dims — e.g., for a 13B model with seq len 2048, each cache entry might be ~1.2-1.8MB. our default cache eviction is LRU with size-based autoscaling; for heavy workloads we recommend dedicated cache nodes in your VPC.
---
09:30 Priya: here's a short worked example. assume 5k daily active users, 3 requests per user per minute during peak, average 64 tokens per request. baseline cost (no batching/no cache) = X token units (~$0.028 per 1k tokens in this hypothetical). with continuous batching you drop to 0.015 per 1k tokens equivalent; add prefix cache and hit rate 12% brings effective cost to ~0.011. numbers in deck are illustrative — we'll run a benchmark on your real traffic.
09:58 Mei: can you share the spreadsheet for these numbers?
10:02 Alex: yes we'll share the cost model spreadsheet and a benchmark harness.
---
12:00 Tom: on the bench harness — do you run p95 and p99 latency so we can see tail? we care about tail.
12:06 Priya: absolutely. our harness outputs p50/p90/p95/p99 and token-level cost, broken down by model variant and batching configuration. we'll include traces and the per-route breakdown.
12:20 Carlos: question: dedicated vs hosted — for sensitive card data we need isolation. do you see customers using Dedicated for that and are there differences for caching?
12:34 Alex: yes many customers with regulated data use Dedicated or Private. caching can be configured inside the dedicated pool and can be provisioned inside your VPC for Private. for hosted we have encrypted-at-rest and can support customer-managed KMS via integration in some plans.
12:52 Mei: does dedicated lower latency? we want predictable p95 at scale.
12:56 Priya: Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and more predictable jitter; if you need sub-200ms at peak it's usually easier on Dedicated because you control GPU pools and autoscale policies.
13:12 Alex: also with Dedicated you can fix model variants to avoid noisy neighbor model swaps.
---
15:00 Priya: live config walkthrough — here's a typical config we recommend for mariner: continuous batching, batch size cap 32, latency cap 200ms, prefix cache TTL 6 hours, cache node pool sized for expected hit rate and 2x headroom.
15:25 Priya: tradeoffs: reduce batch size if you see increased p95; increase cache hit ratio by normalizing prompts and tokenization; consider quantized model variants to save GPU memory and cost.
15:40 Tom: when you say normalizing prompts — can you be concrete?
15:45 Priya: e.g., canonicalize transaction metadata ordering, strip non-deterministic fields, and use stable system prompts so the prefix is identical across requests. small template differences kill cache hits.
16:02 Carlos: what about cache warm-up — will we see a cold-start spike?
16:08 Priya: yes warm-up exists; typical strategy: pre-populate common prefixes during deploy, or ramp traffic gradually. our runtime supports pre-warming APIs.
---
18:30 Alex: now on cost model sensitivity. we showed a few scenarios. at your average token sizes and RPS, the biggest lever is batching early; even a modest batch efficiency improves unit economics more than a small improvement in cache hit rate. cache compounds that.
18:52 Mei: can you show an example where caching hurts latency?
19:00 Priya: caching adds a lookup step — if your cache is remote with network hops it can add 10-30ms. that's why collocating cache (VPC or same cluster) is recommended for low latency SLOs. if cache miss rates are high, the extra hop is wasted.
19:22 Tom: any security risk with cache entries? like PII?
19:28 Alex: cache entries are encrypted and we can redact sensitive fields before caching — e.g., token-level hashing, or avoid caching PII entirely. we'll work with your security team on policy.
---
22:00 Priya: quick demo of benchmark results from a previous customer (anonymized). left chart shows p95 latency by batch size, right chart cost per 1k tokens. you can see sweet spot around batch 16-32 for similar traffic patterns.
22:30 Carlos: will that chart translate to our models? we use a custom 7B with a few fine-tuned heads.
22:38 Priya: mostly yes; kernel selection and quantization matter, but the shape is similar. we'll run the harness against your tuned model image in the POC.
---
25:00 Alex: ok security/compliance checklist — SOC2 Type II, SAML/SSO, RBAC, KMS integration, audit logs retention options. Mei, any specific compliance reqs beyond standard SOC2?
25:12 Mei: we need encryption in customer-managed KMS, audit log retention 7 years for financial ops, and the option for Private deployment for card-data flows.
25:25 Alex: got it. we'll attach our SOC2 and a note on KMS integration; Private deployment is available and our on-prem install can be air-gapped if needed.
---
28:30 Priya: open Q&A. Tom: operationally, how do you handle autoscale and spikes?
28:36 Priya: runtime autoscale uses a combination of queue depth and latency SLOs; for Dedicated you can reserve burst capacity and set conservative scale-up thresholds. we also provide fallback policies that route to a cheaper model variant if primary is saturated.
28:55 Tom: and how is model variant fallback controlled?
29:00 Alex: rollouts are policy-driven — canary, A/B, percentage-based, or automatic fallback when error rates or latencies exceed thresholds. you get per-route dashboards.
---
32:10 Priya: last section: POC plan. 1) exchange traffic profile and sample requests 2) Redwood provides benchmark harness and config 3) Mariner runs harness in a dedicated trial (hosted dedicated or private) 4) analyze p95/p99, cost numbers, iterate. goal: produce a recommendation and cost per 1M requests. estimated time: 2 weeks.
32:40 Mei: timeline sounds fine — we have exec review May 27. can we get numbers before then?
32:47 Alex: we'll prioritize — if we get traffic profile today we can run an initial quick bench and share preliminary numbers by May 20.
---
35:00 Carlos: any vendor lock-in risks with prefix cache format? if we move away later, how portable are entries?
35:12 Priya: cache entries are model-and-runner-specific because KV structure depends on model dims. we provide export tools and guidelines, but full portability isn't guaranteed. for portability, use caching at the application layer with hashed precomputed responses.
35:30 Carlos: ok noted.
---
38:00 Alex: recap and next steps — we'll send the cost model spreadsheet, benchmark script, SOC2 & KMS docs, and a proposed POC plan. Priya will share configs. Mei will send traffic profile. schedule follow-up POC scoping week of May 24.
38:25 Mei: ok thanks.
38:30 Tom: thanks all.
38:33 Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and links.
38:40 (call ends)
